generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, the first stage of writing is reading the task closely. A brief such as 'Evaluate explanations for conformity' has a steer ('evaluate', which asks you to weigh, not just describe) and keywords ('explanations', 'conformity') that fix the topic. A rough plan then bridges your reading of the studies and the writing itself, and a first draft turns that plan into sentences you can improve. Missing the steer is one of the most common and costly mistakes in psychology essays.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students are set the same essay: 'Evaluate explanations for conformity.'

Tom reads the title once, spots the topic, and starts writing everything he knows about conformity. He makes no plan and pays no attention to the word 'evaluate', so the essay becomes a long description of studies that never weighs the explanations against each other. The steer was missed, and a lot of effort goes into answering a question that was not asked.

Amara reads the title closely, underlines 'evaluate' and 'conformity', and notes that the essay must weigh the explanations rather than just list the studies. A quick plan sets out two explanations, their evidence, and an order. Then she writes a rough draft straight from the plan, not worrying yet about style, ready to improve it next.

Both students knew the studies. Only Amara read the task, planned, and turned that plan into a draft, the moves that make the writing answer the question.
generatedProse.summary: Writing in psychology starts with understanding the task: its steer, which tells you how to answer, and its keywords, which fix what to answer. A rough plan then bridges your reading and your writing, and a first draft turns that plan into sentences you can improve. You can now read a psychology brief for its steer and keywords, turn a plan into a draft, and make a sensible first move at the blank page. The next lesson is about improving that draft.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do to turn her understanding into a draft?

items.text: She made a rough plan from the task and wrote a first draft straight from that plan.
She wrote down everything she knew about conformity without a plan.
She polished her opening paragraph until it was perfect before continuing.
She waited until she fully understood the topic before writing anything.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara planned from the task and drafted straight from the plan.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan-then-draft move, rather than a plan-free dump or endless polishing.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara made a rough plan and wrote a draft from it. Writing without a plan, perfecting one paragraph, or waiting indefinitely are not it.
